inputs.sbc_source: FPH.NZ_Metrics.csv StockBasedComp FY2026 (cash flow statement add-back); equity_award_taxes KPI = 0 (no net-share settlement tax withholding disclosed — FPH issues via DRP/employee share schemes, not net-settled RSUs)
inputs.interest_income_treatment: Stripped from owner FCF. Net cash (NZ$401.3m) / FCF base (NZ$468.0m) = 0.86x, just under the project's 1x materiality threshold, but interest income (NZ$8.2m, <2% of FCF) is stripped anyway for consistency since net cash is added back to enterprise value at the end of the DCF — avoids any double count and the amount is immaterial either way.
inputs.sbc_memo_note: If SBC were treated as a non-cash cost (no FCF deduction, no dilution), base-case IV would be $22.21 vs $21.47 actual — a spread of $0.74/share. SBC is small for FPH (0.6% of revenue) so this spread is minor, unlike SBC-heavy tech names.

historical_growth.notes: Standard trailing 3yr/5yr CAGR windows are unusable for FPH: any window starting or ending in FY2021/FY2022 is COVID-hardware-pull-forward distorted (5yr revenue CAGR of only 3.2% reflects the post-COVID consumables/utilisation normalization, not a growth slowdown), and the 3yr window (13.4%) is inflated by the low FY2023 base. Per ticker guidance, the FY2019->FY2026 through-cycle CAGR (spanning one full pre-COVID to post-COVID cycle) is used instead: revenue 11.6%, EPS 11.8%, shareholders' equity 12.8%, NPAT 12.2% — all clustered within a few points of each other (no >30% divergence flag needed). FY2024 NPAT/EPS (7.6% margin, 22.8cps) is a genuine reported low from a product recall + $98.1m land revaluation charge + an NZ building-depreciation tax law change; FPH's own underlying NPAT for FY2024 was $264.4m (15.2% margin) — the through-cycle CAGR calc uses reported FY2026 vs reported FY2019 endpoints so this one-off does not touch the anchor years, but readers should not mistake FY2024 for a genuine cyclical trough when eyeballing the raw series.

wacc_rationale: FPH is a NZ$18-19bn large-cap, one of the NZX's biggest constituents, with a net cash balance sheet (NZ$401.3m net cash at FY2026, gearing -22.8%) and minimal financial leverage. This argues for a cost-of-equity-anchored WACC in the 8.5-10% range, well below what a small/micro-cap NZX name would carry (no illiquidity or thin-float premium is appropriate here — FPH trades with deep liquidity on both NZX and ASX). Base case uses 9.0%, reflecting: (a) NZ risk-free rate + equity risk premium consistent with a global medical-device compounder, (b) a modest premium for FX translation risk given ~99% of revenue is non-NZD (USD ~50%, EUR ~19-20%) against a NZD/MXN cost base with hedge cover thinning materially beyond FY2028-29, and (c) US tariff/trade-policy exposure (90bps FY2026 margin drag, ~50bps guided FY2027, with further escalation risk flagged by management). Bull case uses 8.0% (lower execution/FX risk perceived), bear case 10.5% (FX and tariff risks fully priced, competitive/regulatory risk premium added).

base.entry_price_correction_note: Terminal value rebuilt at the hurdle rate 2026-09-01: min(Gordon@hurdle, cap x FCF_N). The superseded value held the WACC-built terminal value and varied only the discounting.

sanity_check.methodology: 10yr monthly closes from Yahoo Finance (FPH.NZ), aligned to March fiscal year-end close for each FY. FY2021/FY2022 (COVID hardware pull-forward) and FY2024 (product recall + $98.1m land revaluation + NZ depreciation tax-law change) excluded from averages but retained in the table.

FY2024.excluded: recall + land revaluation + tax law change depressed reported NPAT; underlying P/E ~56.7x

sanity_check.notes: Current market price (P/E 53.4x, P/B 11.8x, EV/EBITDA 30.9x, P/S 10.8x) trades essentially IN LINE with FPH's own historical average premium multiples (ex-COVID/FY24: P/E 50.6x, P/B 11.2x, EV/EBITDA 30.6x, P/S 9.8x) — the market is not currently pricing FPH at an unusual extreme versus its own history. The base-case DCF's implied multiples (P/E 26.9x, P/B 6.0x, EV/EBITDA 15.4x, P/S 5.5x) sit well BELOW both the historical average and the current price. Per the ticker-specific guidance for this valuation, this is the expected and correct sanity-check outcome for FPH: the check exists to catch implied multiples that are IMPLAUSIBLY HIGH versus history (i.e., a DCF that has over-shot on optimism), and it PASSES cleanly here because the implied multiples are conservative, not inflated. No assumptions were adjusted to close this gap.

valuation_philosophy.summary: Fisher & Paykel Healthcare has traded at a persistent, structural premium (historically 30-60x trailing P/E, ~9-14x EV/Sales-equivalent, high-single-digit to low-teens P/B) for essentially its entire listed history on the NZX, reflecting its status as one of the exchange's highest-quality, most durable global compounders: razor/razorblade consumables economics (~90% of Hospital and ~88% of Homecare revenue recurring), genuine multi-decade clinical-practice-change growth drivers largely independent of the admissions cycle, a fortress net-cash balance sheet, and scarcity value as one of very few globally-relevant, large-cap growth names available to NZX investors.
valuation_philosophy.why_a_conventional_dcf_undervalues_fph: A component-built, conservative owner-FCF DCF using a large-cap-appropriate 9.0% WACC and a 3.5% terminal growth rate produces a base-case intrinsic value of $21.47/share, roughly 50% below the $42.58 market price. This gap is NOT a modelling defect — it is the honest output of capitalizing FPH's cash flows at a market-consistent discount rate. The market has been willing, for a decade-plus, to pay for FPH's growth and quality using an implicit return expectation well below what a bottom-up DCF discount rate demands (i.e., to accept a lower forward IRR than 9% in exchange for owning a scarce, high-quality compounding asset). This is directly analogous to how a conventional DCF systematically undervalues other structurally premium-rated compounders (e.g., historically MCO, IDXX, or on the NZX, previously observed with other scarce quality names) — it is a known and accepted limitation of DCF applied to businesses the market persistently prices on scarcity/quality grounds rather than on a bottom-up discounted-cash-flow basis.
valuation_philosophy.guidance_followed: Per explicit ticker-specific instruction for this valuation: report the DCF result honestly rather than reverse-engineering assumptions (e.g., an unjustifiably low WACC or an inflated terminal growth rate) to manufacture upside that would not survive scrutiny. The sensitivity table and bull case show the assumption combinations that would be required to close the gap to market (e.g., WACC ~7% with 4%+ terminal growth in the bull scenario approaches, but does not fully reach, the current price) — readers should treat the DCF as a floor/conservative-case anchor and the market price as reflecting an ongoing scarcity/quality premium that a cash-flow-only framework does not capture.
valuation_philosophy.recommendation_framing: This is not a 'sell' signal in isolation — it is a statement that FPH's current price embeds a persistent premium multiple that has actually PERSISTED across a full decade of market history (per the sanity check above, the current multiple is in line with, not above, FPH's own historical average). Investors should weigh the DCF's conservative floor against the company's demonstrated multi-decade ability to sustain premium multiples, rather than treating the DCF gap as evidence of overvaluation on its own.
